title: Channel Coding via Robust Optimization Part 2: The Multi-User Channel
contribution: Writes optimal finite-length channel coding on multi-user Gaussian interference and broadcast channels as optimization problems (rank-constrained SDPs for Gaussian noise, MILPs for exponential and uniform noise) whose values bound the capacity region, reporting a valid lower bound and an approximate upper bound at n = 60 (abstract).
problem_entry: {RO CP IO; AP} Optimal finite-length (n) coding on multi-user Gaussian channels at error probability epsilon; capacity regions of such channels are open (abstract).
key_idea: Optimization formulations whose optimal values give exact upper and lower capacity bounds for finite n, meeting as n tends to infinity; the class follows the noise distribution (abstract).
assumptions: Multi-user Gaussian interference and broadcast channels; finite code length n; error probability bound; Gaussian, exponential and uniform noise (abstract).
proof_devices: rank minimization under semidefinite constraints, attacked by iteratively solving SDPs (abstract)
mixed-integer linear formulations for exponential and uniform noise, solved with commercial solvers (abstract)
experiments: n = 60, two-user Gaussian interference channels; not solved to provable optimality (abstract).
positioning: Part 2 of a two-part manuscript; Part 1 is S554 (title; INDEX).
writing: The abstract states the missing certificate plainly (abstract).
limits_future: Size prevents provable optimality: valid lower bound from a feasible code, upper bound only approximated (abstract).

method_links.note: A problem owned by information theory rewritten as SDP/MIO, with the class traced to the noise model.
The abstract says which bound is certified (the feasible code's lower bound) and which is only approximated.

transferable: When the exact model is too large to certify, state in the abstract which bound remains valid (the feasible solution's) and label the other as an approximation (abstract).

quotes.text: Because of the size and complexity of these formulations, we do not solve them to provable optimality.
Still we provide a feasible code that leads to a valid lower bound on the capacity region, but we only provide approximations for the upper bound on the capacity region.

title: The rise and fall of the model for end-stage liver disease score and the need for an optimized machine learning approach for liver allocation
contribution: Review arguing that MELD-based liver allocation remains inequitable and that OPOM, Optimal Classification Trees predicting 3-month waitlist mortality or removal, prioritizes candidates more accurately and, in simulation, saves additional lives each year (abstract).
problem_entry: {DA ML AP} MELD has ranked candidates since 2002 but, despite revisions, does not give equitable access to all waitlisted candidates (abstract).
key_idea: OPOM: OCT models trained to predict 3-month waitlist mortality or removal, used for prioritization (abstract).
experiments: More accurate and objective prioritization than MELD and MELD-Na; simulation: more equitable allocation and a significant number of additional lives saved per year; no numbers in the abstract (abstract).
positioning: MELD and MELD-Na as incumbent rules (abstract).
writing: Structured review abstract (Purpose of review / Recent findings / Summary); rise-and-fall framing of the incumbent score (title; abstract).
limits_future: ML could guide transplant practice and national allocation policy (abstract).

method_links.note: Incumbent rule (MELD, MELD-Na) as baseline and a decision-level claim (allocation simulation, lives saved), not only accuracy.

coauthors: P. A. Vagefi, R. Hirose, N. Trichakis

quotes.text: When compared to MELD and MELD-Na, OPOM more accurately and objectively prioritized candidates for liver transplantation based on disease severity.
In simulation analysis, OPOM allowed for more equitable allocation of livers with a resultant significant number of additional lives saved every year when compared with MELD-based allocation.

title: Novel machine learning proves stroke risk is not linear
contribution: Meeting abstract of the non-linear stroke risk score: Optimal Classification Trees trained on Framingham offspring examinations and validated at Boston Medical Center beat the revised Framingham score on c-statistic, find 23 risk profiles and ship as an online questionnaire (abstract).
problem_entry: {ML AP; DA} Stroke risk tools presume linear, cumulative risk factors, hiding new factors and interactions; improve on the revised Framingham Stroke Risk Score (abstract).
key_idea: OCT model of 10-year stroke risk, externally validated, delivered as an interactive online questionnaire (abstract).
assumptions: 14,196 training samples with each clinical examination treated as an independent observation; 17,527 validation observations from Boston Medical Center (abstract).
experiments: c-statistic training 87.43% vs 73.74%; validation 75.29% vs 65.93%, also in multi-ethnic populations; 23 risk profiles; new non-linear relations (T-wave abnormality, hematocrit) (abstract).
positioning: Against the revised Framingham Stroke Risk Score (abstract).
writing: Claim in the title ("proves stroke risk is not linear") (title).
limits_future: Prioritizing risk-factor modification and personalized prevention (abstract). Full paper: S189.

method_links.note: The field's incumbent score is the baseline on its own metric with external validation, but predictions, not decisions, are scored.

title: Early Detection of Opioid Over-Procurement: A Machine Learning Approach
contribution: Working-paper version (2020) of S622: machine-learning models on administrative data detect illicit opioid purchasing with high accuracy, years in advance, and could have prevented the illegal distribution of up to 600 million pills in 2006-2012 (abstract).
problem_entry: {ML AP; DA} Prescription-opioid misuse as the leading cause of the decline in US life expectancy; detect diversion across the supply chain (abstract).
key_idea: Machine-learning models on a large volume of administrative data flag suspicious opioid purchasing (abstract).
assumptions: Administrative data on the prescription-drug supply chain (abstract); details not in the abstract.
experiments: High accuracy; early detection up to several years ahead; counterfactual estimate of up to 600 million pills (2006-2012); data source, baselines and metrics not in the abstract (abstract).
writing: Opens with the public-health stakes; headline counterfactual number (abstract).
limits_future: Promise for detecting, preventing and investigating diversion (abstract); published later, retitled, as S622 (MSOM 2025).

method_links.note: Value stated in decision terms (pills that action could have prevented), but the owner (enforcement agency) and its current rule are not named and nothing is field-tested.

quotes.text: We estimate that the implementation of our machine learning models could have prevented the illegal distribution of as many as 600 million pills between 2006 and 2012.
We show that the algorithms can detect illicit opioid transactions with high accuracy, and are capable of early detection up to several years in advance.
